hints.title: Distinct Daily Activity
hints.text: First isolate unique customer and transaction date pairs to avoid double counting multiple purchases in a single day.

hints.title: Consecutive Date Grouping
hints.text: Subtract each row number sequence from the calendar date to produce an identical identifier for consecutive dates.

hints.title: Streak Maximization
hints.text: Aggregate over customer and streak group to calculate streak lengths, then filter customers who achieve the global maximum length.

hints.title: Gaps and Islands Solution
hints.text:
```mysql
WITH UniqueTransactions AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, transaction_date
    FROM Transactions
),
RankedTransactions AS (
    SELECT 
        customer_id,
        transaction_date,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS rn
    FROM UniqueTransactions
),
ConsecutiveGroups AS (
    SELECT 
        customer_id,
        DATE_SUB(transaction_date, INTERVAL rn DAY) AS streak_group,
        COUNT(*) AS consecutive_count
    FROM RankedTransactions
    GROUP BY customer_id, streak_group
),
MaxStreaks AS (
    SELECT 
        customer_id,
        MAX(consecutive_count) AS max_streak
    FROM ConsecutiveGroups
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
GlobalMax AS (
    SELECT MAX(max_streak) AS global_max
    FROM MaxStreaks
)
SELECT m.customer_id
FROM MaxStreaks m
JOIN GlobalMax g ON m.max_streak = g.global_max
ORDER BY m.customer_id ASC;
```

complexity.time: O(N log N) for window ranking and grouping
complexity.notes: Classic gaps and islands pattern using date arithmetic on row number.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Self-joining consecutive days creates combinatorial blowup on dense transaction histories.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Window function partitions customer dates linearly.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Applies standard date minus row-number transformation for consecutive sequences.

WITH UniqueTransactions AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, transaction_date
    FROM Transactions
),
RankedTransactions AS (
    SELECT 
        customer_id,
        transaction_date,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS rn
    FROM UniqueTransactions
),
ConsecutiveGroups AS (
    SELECT 
        customer_id,
        transaction_date - (rn || ' days')::interval AS streak_group,
        COUNT(*) AS consecutive_count
    FROM RankedTransactions
    GROUP BY customer_id, streak_group
),
MaxStreaks AS (
    SELECT 
        customer_id,
        MAX(consecutive_count) AS max_streak
    FROM ConsecutiveGroups
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
GlobalMax AS (
    SELECT MAX(max_streak) AS global_max
    FROM MaxStreaks
)
SELECT m.customer_id
FROM MaxStreaks m
JOIN GlobalMax g ON m.max_streak = g.global_max
ORDER BY m.customer_id ASC;

import pandas as pd

def find_customers(transactions: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = transactions[['customer_id', 'transaction_date']].drop_duplicates().sort_values(['customer_id', 'transaction_date'])
    df['transaction_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['transaction_date'])
    df['rn'] = df.groupby('customer_id').cumcount()
    df['streak_group'] = df['transaction_date'] - pd.to_timedelta(df['rn'], unit='D')
    grouped = df.groupby(['customer_id', 'streak_group']).size().reset_index(name='consecutive_count')
    max_streaks = grouped.groupby('customer_id')['consecutive_count'].max().reset_index(name='max_streak')
    if max_streaks.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame(columns=['customer_id'])
    global_max = max_streaks['max_streak'].max()
    res = max_streaks[max_streaks['max_streak'] == global_max][['customer_id']].sort_values('customer_id')
    return res
